name: Afghanistan
summary: Under Taliban rule, Afghanistan has become the world's most severe women's rights crisis. Girls are banned from secondary education, women are barred from most employment and public life, and over 22 million people — including nearly 5 million children — face acute hunger after mass aid cuts and the forced expulsion of millions of Afghans from neighboring countries.
context:
Since the Taliban's return to power in August 2021, Afghanistan has undergone a systematic dismantling of women's and girls' rights unprecedented in the modern era. Girls have been banned from attending secondary school and university for over four years — the only country in the world with such a prohibition. Women are barred from working in most sectors, prohibited from appearing in public without a male guardian, and banned from raising their voices in public spaces.

The economic and humanitarian consequences are catastrophic. Over 22 million people need humanitarian assistance, and 17.4 million face acute food insecurity. Nearly 5 million children are acutely malnourished. The Taliban's restrictions have also devastated the healthcare system: women cannot be treated by male doctors in many areas, yet female healthcare workers have been dismissed, causing maternal mortality to rise sharply.

Massive US aid cuts and the subsequent collapse of humanitarian funding have compounded the crisis. In 2025, 422 health facilities closed due to funding shortfalls. Simultaneously, Iran and Pakistan have forcibly expelled over 2 million Afghan refugees, adding to an already overwhelmed population.

The UN has described Afghanistan's situation as 'gender apartheid' — a crime against humanity. UN Women projects that the education bans will increase child marriage by 25%, adolescent childbearing by 45%, and maternal mortality by at least 50%. A full generation of Afghan girls is being systematically denied the right to an education and a future.

Despite calls from the international community, the Taliban has shown no signs of reversing its policies. Afghanistan remains largely inaccessible for independent human rights monitoring.

awareness: Share the reality that Afghanistan is the only country on Earth where girls are banned from secondary school and university — a policy in effect for over four years
Amplify the voices of Afghan women activists, journalists, and scholars who have fled and continue to speak out from abroad
Highlight that the aid funding collapse — not just Taliban policy — is killing Afghan children through preventable malnutrition and disease
Challenge the framing that Afghanistan is a 'solved' problem — it is the world's most severe ongoing women's rights emergency
Support organizations providing education to Afghan girls via online and underground programs
political: Demand that your government condition any diplomatic engagement with the Taliban on tangible progress for girls' education and women's rights
Urge representatives to restore and increase humanitarian aid to Afghanistan through neutral organizations, with strict safeguards against Taliban diversion
Support calls for the UN to formally recognize gender apartheid as a crime against humanity — Afghanistan is the defining case
Push for expanded refugee resettlement quotas for Afghan women, girls, journalists, and human rights defenders
Demand accountability for countries forcibly expelling Afghan refugees who face persecution upon return
